extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent agents/attorneys, and examiners practicing under Indian patent law
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on substantive patentability exclusions, disclosure/unity requirements, examination/FER procedures, pre- and post-grant opposition practice, grant consequences, and related prosecution rules under Indian law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere admixture not patentable (Section 3(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: A substance obtained by a mere admixture resulting only in the aggregation of the properties of the components thereof or a process for producing such substance is not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An admixture resulting in synergistic properties is not considered a mere admixture and may be patentable (examples: soap, detergent, lubricant and polymer compositions). The application should clearly bring out synergistic effect by way of comparison at the time of filing. Subsequent submissions regarding synergism can be accepted in reply to office action as supporting evidence but such submitted data cannot become part of the Specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere arrangement/re-arrangement/duplication not patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere arrangement or re-arrangement or duplication of known devices each functioning independently of one another in a known way is not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be patentable, an improvement or combination must be more than a workshop improvement and must satisfy inventive step. The combination should produce a new result, new article, or a better/cheaper article. Mere collocation of items without working interrelation (e.g., juxtaposition where each element functions independently) is not patentable. Where old integers when combined have working interrelation producing new or improved results, subject-matter may be patentable (multiple case law examples given).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of agriculture or horticulture not patentable (Section 3(h))
rubrics_metrics.description: A method of agriculture or horticulture is not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: method of producing a new form of a known plant by modifying conditions, method of producing improved soil using certain treatments, method of producing mushrooms, method for cultivation of algae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of medical/therapeutic/diagnostic/surgical treatment not patentable (Section 3(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: Any process for the medicinal, surgical, curative, prophylactic, diagnostic, therapeutic or other treatment of human beings or any process for a similar treatment of animals is not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: medicinal administration methods (oral, injectable, topical, patches), surgical methods (e.g., stitch-free incision for cataract removal), curative methods (vaccination), prophylactic methods (teeth cleaning method), diagnostic methods performed on the human/animal body (requires deductive step and specific interactions with body to fall under prohibition). Exclusions include cosmetic procedures, termination of pregnancy, sterilization, artificial insemination, embryo transplants, removal of organs from living donor, etc. Instruments/apparatus, prostheses, artificial limbs and measurements on the human body are patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plants, animals and essentially biological processes not patentable (Section 3(j))
rubrics_metrics.description: Plants and animals in whole or any part thereof other than micro-organisms (including seeds, varieties and species) and essentially biological processes for production or propagation of plants and animals are not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Microorganisms and microbiological processes are patentable but a microorganism merely discovered in nature is not. New processes of preparation (e.g., vaccine preparation under defined conditions) may be patentable. Plant varieties are protected under a different statute (Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2002).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical methods, business methods, computer programs per se and algorithms not patentable (Section 3(k))
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical methods, business methods, computer programmes per se and algorithms are not considered patentable inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details: mathematical methods are acts of mental faculty and not patentable; business methods (commerce-related activities) are excluded even if implemented with internet/technical features if in substance they are business methods; computer programme products stored on a medium (program per se) are not allowable. However, claims not directed at computer programme per se could be patentable if other conditions met. For method claims involving computer programmes to be patentable they must clearly recite limiting hardware integers enabling the program to function; programs that work on general-purpose computers typically fail. Algorithm claims that merely express general principles (allowing different programs) are not patentable. Computer programs coupled to hardware that enable hardware to perform a function may be allowable if all patentability conditions are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary, dramatic, musical or artistic works not patentable (Section 3(l))
rubrics_metrics.description: A literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work or any other aesthetic creation whatsoever including cinematographic works and television productions is not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List of excluded items: writings, music, fine arts, paintings, sculptures, computer programmes (note overlap with other provisions), electronic databases, books, lectures, dramatic-musical works, choreography, cinematographic works, drawings, architecture, photographs, applied art, illustrations, maps, translations, adaptations, multimedia productions. Such works fall under Copyright Act, 1957.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheme/rule/mental act/method of playing game not patentable (Section 3(m))
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere scheme or rule or method of performing mental act or method of playing game is not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: method of playing chess, method of teaching, method of learning, method of operating a machine or equipment as per set of instructions when outcome is a mental process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation of information not patentable (Section 3(n))
rubrics_metrics.description: Any manner, means or method of expressing information whether visual, audible or tangible (words, codes, signals, symbols, diagrams or any other mode) is not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: speech instruction in printed text with underlining and separation marks, railway timetable, 100-year calendar. Business method claims and methods of presenting information are commonly disallowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topography of integrated circuits not patentable (Section 3(o))
rubrics_metrics.description: Topography (layout designs) of integrated circuits is not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Layout designs of integrated circuits are governed by the Semiconductor Integrated Circuit Lay-out Designs Act, 2000, so three-dimensional configurations used in microchips/semiconductor chips are excluded from patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditional knowledge, aggregation/duplication of traditional components not patentable (Section 3(p))
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention which is traditional knowledge or an aggregation/duplication of known properties of traditionally known components is not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: antiseptic properties of turmeric, pesticidal properties of neem. Examiners should consult the Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) and other resources to decide whether claimed subject-matter falls under this provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of disclosure — title requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must be properly titled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the Examiner's sufficiency of disclosure check; title should accurately reflect the subject-matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of disclosure — full and particular description
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject matter must be fully and particularly described in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner checks that the specification enables a person skilled in the art to understand and carry out the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of disclosure — claims must define scope properly
rubrics_metrics.description: The claims should define the scope of the invention properly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims are examined to ensure they are clear, supported by description, and delimit the monopoly sought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of disclosure — best method disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: The Specification must describe the best method of performing the invention, if any is known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omission of the best method can lead to objection for insufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of disclosure — biological materials source and origin
rubrics_metrics.description: For inventions related to biological materials, the source and geographical origin must be disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner verifies disclosure of origin where applicable (related to access and benefit-sharing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of disclosure — Biodiversity Authority approval and depository details
rubrics_metrics.description: Approval obtained from the Biodiversity Authority, where applicable, and accession number and depository details (where relevant) should be disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Required for biological inventions relying on biological resources; omission can be an objection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of invention — single inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: The claims of a specification shall relate to a single inventive concept; where multiple inventive concepts are present examiner will report plurality and application may be divided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination of linkage to form single general inventive concept is without regard to claim drafting format (separate claims or alternatives). Division can be required to cure plurality. Examples illustrate when product/process/apparatus claims may be considered a single invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of invention — process and apparatus linkage
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity between process and apparatus requires that the apparatus or means have been specifically designed for carrying out the process, or at least a step of the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independent claims of different categories may nonetheless relate to single inventive concept (e.g., product and specially adapted manufacturing process; process and apparatus specifically designed for it). Examples 1–8 provided (product/process/mould/locking system/broadcasting system/spray bottle/drug and related claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: FER timelines and contents
rubrics_metrics.description: The Controller considers the examiner's report ordinarily within one month and sends a First Examination Report (FER) with a gist of objections to the applicant; FER may contain office objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FER may include objections on lack of novelty, inventive step, industrial applicability; subject-matter falling under Section 3 and 4; and non-fulfillment of other Act requirements. FER is sent even when examination requested by third party; applicant must respond to requirements communicated via FER.

rubrics_metrics.name: Response to FER — 12-month abandonment risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant must comply with all requirements communicated through FER or subsequent communication within twelve months from forwarding of FER, failing which application is deemed abandoned under Section 21(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If re-filed after 12 months for reasons beyond control, Controller may proceed based on evidence of delay; when re-filed within 12 months the examiner examines afresh. No appeal against abandonment order under this Section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-dating of application (Section 17)
rubrics_metrics.description: Application may be post-dated to a date not later than six months from the date of application on request before grant, subject to prescribed fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If request made before examination it may be allowed and examination conducted with reference to post-dated filing date. If after FER, allowed subject to fresh examination. Controller may deem amendments to have been made on date requirements complied with; examples include bringing in missing parts or new drawings to explain amended specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-grant opposition — who/how/when (Section 25(1), Rule 55)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person can file opposition by representation after publication under Section 11A but before grant on grounds in Section 25(1); pre-grant opposition must be filed within six months from date of publication to ensure it's before grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representation must include statement and evidence (if any) and request for hearing. Controller considers representation only after Request for Examination filed. Pre-grant opposition is considered along with examiner report. If opponent requests hearing and Controller finds opposition devoid of merit, opportunity of hearing will be granted and a speaking order rejecting opposition issued ordinarily within one month; if opposition has merit Controller issues notice to applicant who may reply within three months. Controller then either refuses grant or asks for amendment and will decide ordinarily within one month after proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for grant — compliance with Act and no outstanding objections
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent is granted when application has not been refused and is not in contravention of Act provisions; all examiner objections must be met and FER requirements complied with within timelines; no pre-grant representation pending or pre-grant opposition disposed in favor of applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Date of grant is date on which patent number is generated and patent is granted by Controller.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of grant — public availability and post-grant opposition window
rubrics_metrics.description: On grant: patent given serial number, Certificate of Patent generated, complete specification as granted made available to public, application/specification open for inspection on fee, grant published in official journal, post-grant opposition under Section 25(2) available within 12 months from date of publication of grant, and working statements (Form-27) must be furnished regularly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentee and licensee must furnish statement regarding working of patented invention on commercial scale in India at regular intervals (not less than six months) in prescribed format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date and term of patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Date of patent is the date of filing of the application (for PCT national phase, international filing date). Term of patent is 20 years from filing date provided annual renewal fees paid timely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time for payment of renewal fee reckoned from date of recordal in register (now same as date of generation of Certificate due to electronic processing). Extended period max six months for renewal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights of patentee (Section 48)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a patented product, patentee has exclusive right to prevent third parties from making, using, offering for sale, selling or importing that product in India. For a patented process, patentee can prevent third parties from using that process and from using/offering/selling/importing the product obtained directly by that process in India.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard territorial/exclusive rights subject to statutory exceptions and limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights of co-owners (Section 50)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a patent is granted to two or more persons, each person is entitled to an equal undivided share unless agreement to contrary; each may exercise rights conferred by Section 48 for his own benefit without accounting to the others, subject to agreements and Sections 51.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licence or assignment of share cannot be granted by one co-owner without consent of others unless agreement says otherwise. Sale by one co-owner gives purchaser same dealing rights as if sold by sole patentee. Rules of ownership/devolution of movable property apply to patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent rights not infringed in certain temporary foreign vehicle cases (Section 49)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a patented invention on board a foreign-registered vessel/aircraft or a land vehicle owned by a person ordinarily resident in such country coming into India temporarily/accidentally is not deemed infringement when used on board for actual needs only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Does not extend to vessels/aircraft/vehicles from countries that do not confer corresponding rights to Indian persons in their jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-grant opposition — filing, interest, and grounds (Section 25(2), Rule 55A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any interested person can file Notice of Opposition within twelve months from date of publication of grant. Opponent must prove interest and opposition can be filed only on grounds mentioned in Section 25(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copy of notice is furnished to patentee; documents must be in duplicate and authenticated; originals or notarized copies required; translations in English with attestation required for non-English documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-grant opposition — patentee reply and default revocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentee desirous of contesting must file reply statement with grounds and evidence within two months from receipt of opponent's written statement and evidence; if patentee does not contest or fails to file reply/evidence within two months, patent deemed revoked and Controller issues revocation order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After patentee reply, opponent may file reply statement and evidence within one month; opponent's reply evidence strictly confined to matters in patentee's evidence. No further evidence except with leave of Controller.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition Board constitution and report (Rules 56-60)
rubrics_metrics.description: After receipt of Notice of Opposition, the Controller constitutes an Opposition Board (three members including a Chairman) to examine the notice and documents and submit a joint recommendation with reasons on each ground within three months from forwarding documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner may be a member but the examiner who dealt with the application during prosecution shall not be included. If further evidence is taken by Controller, it shall be forwarded to Board; same applies if evidence taken after Board report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearing procedures in opposition (Rule 62)
rubrics_metrics.description: Controller fixes hearing date/time without undue delay and informs parties at least ten days in advance; parties desiring to be heard must notify Controller with prescribed fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Controller may require Opposition Board members to be present. Controller may refuse to hear party who hasn't given notice/fee. If either party intends to rely on any publication not already mentioned, they must notify other party and Controller at least five days before hearing with publication details. After hearing (or without hearing if neither desires it) and considering Board recommendation, Controller decides (revoke patent, order amendments, or refuse opposition) and issues a speaking order.
